units.text: Jefferson sent Livingston to France in 1803 to negotiate New Orleans; Monroe joined him later that year. Multiple sources confirm both envoys were active in France in 1803 working on the New Orleans purchase.

citations.title: Robert R. Livingston’s Louisiana Purchase Letter | Historic New Orleans Collection
Robert R. Livingston’s Louisiana Purchase Letter | Historic New Orleans Collection

judgement.reason: The passages support that Jefferson sent Livingston to negotiate New Orleans and that Monroe joined Livingston in Paris on April 12, 1803, but they indicate Livingston was already the resident minister in January 1803, so they do not support that Jefferson sent him to France in 1803.

units.text: Jefferson appointed Monroe as envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary to France in January 1803, and Livingston was the resident minister authorized to purchase territory including New Orleans. Monroe joined Livingston in Paris on April 12 after Livingston's negotiations were well under way

judgement.reason: The passages state Jefferson appointed Monroe in January 1803 as envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary, identify Livingston as resident minister involved in purchasing territory including New Orleans, and state Monroe joined Livingston in Paris on April 12 after negotiations were well under way.

units.text: Livingston was dispatched immediately upon learning Spain had retroceded New Orleans and Louisiana to France, and Monroe's appointment in January 1803 set the diplomatic framework for the New Orleans acquisition

citations.title: Robert R. Livingston’s Louisiana Purchase Letter | Historic New Orleans Collection

judgement.reason: One passage states Jefferson dispatched Livingston immediately upon learning of Spain's retrocession to France, and the Britannica passage confirms Monroe's January 1803 appointment to aid Livingston in purchasing New Orleans and nearby territory, supporting both parts of the statement.
